n: The Preacher decides to test whether pleasure can satisfy. He tells his heart to enjoy itself, but finds pleasure just as fleeting.

f.g: An old phrase meaning “Come now” or “Let’s try.”

n: Laughter and fun, he concludes, are a kind of madness when chased for their own sake. They accomplish nothing lasting.
He experiments with wine and even folly, while trying to keep his mind wise, to discover what is truly good for people in their short lives.

f.g: Still guiding himself by wisdom during the experiment.

n: He turns to great building projects — houses and vineyards. Solomon was known for vast construction, including the temple and his palace.
He plants gardens and orchards full of every kind of fruit tree, creating a kind of paradise for himself.

f.g: Hebrew pardes, a Persian loanword for an enclosed park — the source of our word “paradise.”

n: He builds reservoirs to irrigate forests of young trees. In a dry land, this was a sign of great wealth and engineering.

f.g: Large reservoirs; ancient pools south of Bethlehem are traditionally called “Solomon’s Pools.”

n: He gathers many servants and huge herds, more than anyone before him in Jerusalem. He lacked nothing in possessions.

f.g: Servants whose families had served the household for generations.
Large and small livestock — herds and flocks.

n: He piles up silver, gold, royal treasures, singers, and every kind of entertainment. Every pleasure money could buy was his.

f.g: Special or prized treasure, like tribute from other kings.

n: He became greater than anyone before him, yet he kept his wisdom. He wasn’t lost in pleasure; he was watching it carefully.

f.g: He stayed clear-headed throughout the experiment.

n: He denied himself nothing he wanted, and he did enjoy his work. That enjoyment was the only reward the work gave him.
Looking back at all he built and enjoyed, he found it empty — like chasing the wind. Nothing gave lasting gain.
He turns to compare wisdom with foolishness. Any king after him can only repeat what he has already tried, so his findings stand.

f.g: His successor — no one will have more resources to test life than he did.

n: Wisdom really is better than folly — as much better as light is than darkness. The Preacher doesn’t deny wisdom’s value.
The wise person can see where he is going, while the fool stumbles in the dark. Yet the same fate — death — comes to both.

f.g: He sees clearly and watches his steps.

n: If he will die like the fool anyway, he wonders what good his extra wisdom did him. This too seems empty.
Both wise and foolish are soon forgotten after they die. From an earthly view, death seems to erase every difference.
Seeing this, he felt disgust for life itself, because all earthly work seemed fleeting. He honestly describes a season of despair.
He hated his own achievements because he would have to leave them all to someone else when he died.

f.w: leave it unto the man that shall be after me

n: His heir might be wise or a fool, yet would control everything he built. History shows Solomon’s son Rehoboam lost most of the kingdom through poor judgment.
He let himself sink into despair about all his hard work.

f.g: To give up hope; literally to make his heart lose heart.

n: Someone may work with skill and fairness, only to hand it all to a person who did nothing to earn it. The Preacher calls this a real wrong.
So what does a person really get out of all the toil and anxiety of life?
Work brings sorrow by day and sleepless worry by night. Even rest escapes the anxious worker.
Here is a key insight: the simple ability to enjoy food, drink, and one’s work is a gift from God. Joy comes from His hand, not from striving.
No one has tested enjoyment more than the Preacher, so he speaks from experience: real enjoyment depends on God.
God gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy to those who please Him, while the sinner gathers wealth that ends up with the righteous. Even so, from below life still feels fleeting.

f.w: giveth to a man that is good
